name: Uma Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm not much of a talker, but I'll try. I've only got till the evening feed, mind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and out to the cattle shed at Brookfield by six. Walter and June Halloran own it, sixty suckler cows, about two hundred ewes and some barley and turnips. I muck out, fork silage, check the water troughs, and in spring I'm in the lambing shed half the night. I like the animals more than people, honestly, and I hate the paperwork days when June asks me to fill in the movement forms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay wears me out more than the work. I get the lowest rate Walter can get away with, and I rent the little room over the old dairy from them, so the rent comes straight off my wages. What I like is the quiet in the shed at night when a ewe's lambed fine and everything's settled. I've got about three weeks of money in the bank, if that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype, then. That sounds about right to me, I've never seen a computer muck out a shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the market everyone's on about clever apps, and the Hallorans' grandson keeps showing June things on his phone. I'd tell them a cow still calves at three in the morning whether there's an app or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't take my worries away, because my worries were never about computers. Walter's sixty-nine and his knees are gone, and June keeps saying they might sell up to the big estate next door. If Brookfield goes, my job goes and my room goes the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and try to put fifty a month by, though most months I can't. I'd go to the farmworkers' union meeting in the market town again, the one I keep missing, because they talk about tied housing. And I'd ask June straight out what the plan is when they retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the same knot I already carry. The AI bit doesn't scare me, it's the selling-up bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the room comes with the job. What would happen if Brookfield sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have nowhere to sleep, simply that. My mum's got a one-bed flat in town above the chemist and she'd say come home, but I'd be on her sofa at twenty-seven. If the Hallorans sell the farm, I lose my wages and my bed in the same week. That's the bit nobody at the market talks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that worry, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Walter and June, they've been decent to me. I blame the way land goes to whoever's biggest, like the Castleford estate that keeps buying farms around us. Small farms get swallowed and the workers just get handed a week's notice. A proper union with some teeth would help people like me.

say: I'd say **AI hype** was never going to muck out a cattle shed.
I'd remind people a cow still **calves at night**, with or without an app.
think: My real worry is the Hallorans **selling Brookfield**, not computers.
If the farm sells, I lose my **job and my room** at once.
do: Try to save **fifty pounds a month**, knowing most months I won't manage it.
Go to the **union meeting** in town about tied housing.
Ask June directly about the **retirement plan** for the farm.
feel: The same **old knot** about money and the farm's future.
Not scared of AI, but **worried** about the selling-up.
S0.quote: If the Hallorans sell the farm, I lose my wages and my bed in the same week.
fieldNote: Uma's **existing pressure** is tied housing: her job and her room depend on one ageing couple.
She dismisses AI quickly, but her **mood is anxious** because of the farm's likely sale.
She blames **land consolidation**, not her employers, and sees the union as the fix.

steps.text: Keep doing the morning and evening feeds at Brookfield
Put fifty pounds a month into savings when the wages allow
Attend the farmworkers' union meeting about tied housing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks, so the forms and the ordering. That's June's side of things, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough for office people, but it's not coming for the lambing shed any time soon. I'd probably say it at the union meeting too, that farm workers are last in line and first forgotten. Online I don't post much, I've got an old phone that barely loads anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think June would love it, because she hates the movement forms and the feed orders. That doesn't touch me much. What touches me is robots coming slowly, because Walter's grandson already talks about a feed-pushing robot like the one on the Castleford dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work hard so I'm the one they keep. I'd stop buying takeaway on Fridays and put that twenty pounds away. And I'd push the union to get something written down about notice and housing for farm workers before the machines turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then annoyed with myself for being uneasy. I don't like change and this is a lot of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used AI tools. Would you try one if June asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. My cousin put one on my phone and I deleted it the same day, it felt like talking to nobody. If June wanted the forms done that way, she'd do them herself, she's better with screens than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a feed-pushing robot mean for your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Feeding is half my morning, so it would take a big bite. Walter would keep me for lambing and the sheep, I think, but maybe not full time. A robot on the feed passage could cut my hours by a third, and a third of nothing much is a lot.

say: I'd say office work changes first and **farm workers** are forgotten.
I'd tell the union farmhands are **last in line** for any help.
think: The forms going to AI is **June's business**, not mine.
A **feed-pushing robot** like Castleford's is what could cut my hours.
do: Work harder so I'm **the one they keep** if hours drop.
Cut the **Friday takeaway** and save that twenty pounds instead.
Push the union for written rules on **notice and housing**.
feel: **Uneasy**, then cross with myself for feeling it.
Tired of how much **change** keeps coming at once.
S1.quote: A robot on the feed passage could cut my hours by a third, and a third of nothing much is a lot.
fieldNote: Uma rejects **AI tools** outright and has deleted one before.
She sees the real threat as **robots on feeding**, half of her morning work.
Her plan is loyalty and the **union**, not new skills, which fits her resistance to change.

steps.text: Keep doing lambing and sheep work so Walter keeps her on
Stop the Friday takeaway and bank the twenty pounds
Push the union for written notice rules for farm housing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I've even saved a month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this needs stopping, or at least slowing down, and the government should make the companies pay for it. I'd say it at the union and I'd sign every petition going. People who own the machines shouldn't get to throw everyone else out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in farming by 2031. The thinking AI in 2028 won't touch me much, I don't do the planning. The robots three years later will do everything I do, and three years is the only cushion I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working while there's work, and save every penny, no going out at all. I'd ask my mum if I could have her box room back if Brookfield lets me go. I'd go to the union every month and push for a payout for farm workers who lose their jobs to machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like standing in a field when the sky goes black before a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What would you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the worst bit. Everyone says retrain, but retrain for what, if AGI is doing all the thinking jobs already. I suppose I'd use the three years to save and to fight, because that's all I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning to run or fix the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm no good with machines that have screens, I struggle with the tractor's new display. Somebody clever from a college will get that job, not me. I'd rather stand at a picket line than pretend I'm a robot engineer.

say: I'd say the companies should **pay** for the workers they replace.
I'd sign every **petition** and say it loudly at the union.
think: I'm **finished in farming** by 2031 when the robots come.
The **three-year gap** is my only cushion, and I don't know how to use it.
do: Save every penny and **stop going out** completely.
Ask my mum about **moving back** into her box room.
Push the union monthly for a **payout** for displaced farm workers.
feel: **Sick** to my stomach, like a storm coming over the field.
S2.quote: The robots three years later will do everything I do, and three years is the only cushion I've got.
fieldNote: Uma sees the **2028 thinking AI** as harmless to her, but the 2031 robots as the end.
She refuses **retraining** because she doesn't trust herself with screens.
Her response is **collective**: petitions, union, compensation, plus falling back on her **mother**.

steps.text: Stop all spending on going out and bank the difference
Ask her mum about moving into the box room in town
Attend every monthly union meeting and push for a payout
Sign petitions calling for companies to pay for replaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking, eight for the robots. Better than two, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that the government has to plan for people like me, not just the clever ones. I'd say we've got time now, so there's no excuse. I'd probably go on about it until people at the market got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight years before robots in the shed buys me something. I'd be thirty-five. I still don't think I'd be in farming at the end of it, but I might have a bit put by and maybe a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work and save, and I'd let the union help me look at what jobs are still around in town. Maybe the care home where my mum works, because robots doing that feels further off. I'd start asking about it in the second or third year, not straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but it's a slower kind of worry. I can breathe a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work. Is that something you'd actually want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd rather be with animals, but my mum's done care work twenty years and the care home always has jobs. I'd do it before I'd sit at home doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Brookfield in this one, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter will be gone by then, one way or another, and June won't keep it going alone. I think the Castleford estate buys it and puts robots in when they arrive. I'd want to be gone before I'm told to go.

say: I'd say with five years there's **no excuse** for doing nothing.
I'd say the government must plan for **farm workers**, not just clever people.
think: Eight years before robots means I'm **thirty-five** when they come.
I probably still **leave farming**, but with a little money and a plan.
do: Keep working and **saving** at Brookfield for now.
Ask in year two or three about **care home jobs** in town.
feel: Still **worried**, but a slower, more breathable kind.
S3.quote: I'd rather be with animals, but my mum's done care work twenty years and the care home always has jobs.
fieldNote: The extra time eases her tone, but she still **expects to lose** farm work by 2034.
She'd consider **care work** only as a fallback, through her mother.
She expects the **Castleford estate** to buy Brookfield and automate it.

steps.text: Keep working at Brookfield and save what she can
Ask about jobs at her mum's care home in year two
Press local councillors to plan for farm workers' jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and then thirteen for the robots. I'd be forty by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's long enough to fix things if anyone bothers. I'd still say the union matters, maybe more. Workers need to be at the table for ten years, not just the last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels like a lifetime to me. By 2039 I might have my own few sheep on rented ground, or I might be doing something else entirely. It's not nothing, but it doesn't keep me up the way two years does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Brookfield as long as it lasts. I'd keep going to the union and maybe get on the branch committee, which I've never had the nerve for. And I'd try to save properly, a little each month, without the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. The money worry is still there whatever year it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money worry stays. What's the money worry right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three weeks of savings and a room that belongs to my boss. If my boot splits or the car fails its test, my savings are gone, whether AGI comes in two years or ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your mind about learning new tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If Walter's grandson showed me something that actually saved me a job, I'd watch. I'm not going to go looking for it, though.

say: I'd say ten years is **long enough** to fix things if anyone tries.
I'd say **workers need a seat** at the table for the whole decade.
think: By **2039** I might have a few sheep or another job.
Ten years doesn't **keep me up** the way two years does.
do: Carry on at **Brookfield** for as long as it lasts.
Try for the union **branch committee** for the first time.
Save a **little each month** without panicking.
feel: **Calmer**, but the money worry never really goes.
Still **uneasy** about a split boot or a failed car test.
S4.quote: If my boot splits or the car fails its test, my savings are gone, whether AGI comes in two years or ten.
fieldNote: The decade **lowers her alarm**, but her thin savings and tied room keep her anxious.
She shows a first small step toward **leadership** in the union.
She'd only consider **new tech** if someone showed her it saved jobs.

steps.text: Keep working at Brookfield while the Hallorans run it
Stand for the union branch committee
Put a small fixed sum aside each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd have nothing saved and nowhere of my own when the robots come. What would help is a real union for farm workers and a proper notice period with housing. Losing the job shouldn't mean losing the roof the same week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the animals. Nobody asks who's going to notice a ewe that's off her feed. A robot might, I suppose, but I'd want to see it first.

headlineQuote: Losing the job shouldn't mean losing the roof the same week.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old farmhand** at Brookfield, a small sheep and suckler-cow farm owned by an ageing couple.
She rents a **tied room** from her employers and has about three weeks of savings.
She avoids **AI tools** entirely and trusts the union more than technology.
Her mood stays **anxious or worse** in every picture, mostly because of the farm's likely sale.
She expects **robots on feeding** to end her job, and sees care work as a reluctant fallback.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive by 2031 before she has savings or a home.
whatWouldHelp: A stronger **farmworkers' union** with written notice rules.
Protection so losing a job doesn't mean **losing housing** the same week.
